question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

ARDUOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Strenuous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Arduous (adjective) means involving great and sustained effort; difficult and tiring. (कठिन, श्रमसाध्य)
◦ Example: The rescue party faced an arduous climb through fresh snow.

 

• Strenuous carries the same sense — requiring or using great exertion. (परिश्रमपूर्ण)
◦ Example: Doctors advised him against strenuous exercise for a month.

 

• The word comes from Latin arduus (steep, high), which is why it suits tasks and journeys that demand prolonged effort rather than a single burst of it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Effortless (सहज, आसान): requiring no exertion — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Trivial (तुच्छ, मामूली): of little value or importance.

 

• Option 4: Soothing (आरामदायक): having a calming effect — again unrelated to effort.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of arduous asked in SSC: laborious, onerous, gruelling, exacting, toilsome.

 

• Antonyms: easy, facile, undemanding, effortless, simple.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

VERBOSE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Concise.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Verbose (adjective) means using far more words than are needed; tediously wordy. (शब्दाडम्बरपूर्ण, वाचाल)
◦ Example: The verbose preface added nothing to the argument of the book.

 

• Concise means giving much information clearly and in few words, and is therefore its direct opposite. (संक्षिप्त)
◦ Example: The committee asked for a concise summary of one page.

 

• The word comes from Latin verbum (word), the same root as verbal, verbatim and verbiage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Wordy (शब्दबहुल): using too many words — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Long-winded (लंबा-चौड़ा, उबाऊ): speaking at tedious length — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Rambling (बिखरा हुआ, असंबद्ध): wandering from point to point without order — again close in sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Three options agree and one stands apart — the odd option is the answer. Other antonyms of verbose: succinct, terse, laconic, pithy, compendious.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To play second fiddle
option_1: To perform a task with great skill
option_2: To take a subordinate position to someone else
option_3: To repeat an argument that has already been made
option_4: To imitate a rival’s methods openly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To take a subordinate position to someone else.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To play second fiddle” means to occupy a lesser or supporting role while another person leads. (गौण भूमिका निभाना)
◦ Example: After leading the department for a decade, he was unwilling to play second fiddle to a junior.

 

• The image comes from the orchestra, in which the second violin supports the melody carried by the first — an essential part, but not the leading one.

 

• The idiom carries a mild suggestion of reluctance; it is generally used of someone who deserves, or wishes for, a larger role.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes skilful performance and merely plays on the literal image of music.

 

• Option 3 describes repetition — “to harp on the same string”.

 

• Option 4 describes imitation — “to take a leaf out of someone’s book”.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of rank and comparison worth revising: to hold a candle to (to compare with), to steal the show (to attract all attention), to call the shots (to be in control), to be a cut above (to be superior to).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

OPULENT
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Destitute.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Opulent (adjective) means displaying great wealth; rich, luxurious and costly. (समृद्ध, वैभवशाली)
◦ Example: The palace was famous for its opulent halls and gilded ceilings.

 

• Destitute means extremely poor and lacking the means of subsistence, and is therefore its direct opposite. (निर्धन, अकिंचन)
◦ Example: The flood left hundreds of families destitute.

 

• The word comes from Latin opes (wealth, resources), the same root as opulence and copious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Lavish (भरपूर, आडम्बरपूर्ण): given or spent in generous, even excessive, quantity — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Affluent (संपन्न): having plenty of money — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Sumptuous (भव्य, आलीशान): splendid and expensive-looking — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of opulent: impoverished, indigent, penurious, needy, austere. Note also the useful pair affluence (wealth) and indigence (poverty).

question: Spot the correct spelling of the process by which a cell engulfs solid particles.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Phagocytosis.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Phagocytosis is the process by which a cell surrounds and takes in solid material such as bacteria or cell debris. (कोशिका द्वारा ठोस कणों का भक्षण)
◦ Example: White blood cells destroy invading bacteria by phagocytosis.

 

• The spelling is fixed by three Greek elements — phago- (eating) + cyt- (cell) + -osis (process). Each part keeps its own letters: phago, then cyt with a ‘c’ and a ‘y’, then the ending -osis.

 

• The same elements recur in cytoplasm, cytology, leucocyte, and in osmosis and metamorphosis for the suffix.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Phagosytosis — an ‘s’ wrongly replaces the ‘c’ of cyt-.

 

• Option 3: Phagocytosys — the suffix must be -osis, never -osys.

 

• Option 4: Phagocitosis — an ‘i’ wrongly replaces the ‘y’ of cyt-.

 

NOTE

 

• Related biological terms tested for spelling: pinocytosis (intake of liquid), photosynthesis, mitosis, meiosis, homeostasis, symbiosis — all ending in -osis or -esis.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: ‘A person who flatters the powerful in order to gain advantage’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Sycophant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A sycophant is a person who praises important people insincerely in order to win their favour. (चापलूस, खुशामदी)
◦ Example: The minister was surrounded by sycophants who agreed with every word he spoke.

 

• The essential elements of the definition are flattery and self-interest; a word denoting mere generosity or solitude cannot satisfy both.

 

• The related adjective is sycophantic, and the everyday equivalents are toady, bootlicker and flatterer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Philanthropist (परोपकारी, दानवीर): one who gives generously to promote human welfare.

 

• Option 3: Recluse (एकांतप्रिय, विरक्त): one who lives alone and avoids the company of others.

 

• Option 4: Altruist (परार्थपरायण व्यक्ति): one who acts for the good of others rather than for himself — the very reverse of self-interest.

 

NOTE

 

• The ‘person who’ cluster set with it: misanthrope (hater of mankind), egotist (one absorbed in himself), opportunist (one who exploits circumstances), demagogue (a leader who appeals to popular passions).

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: ‘A person who knows and can use several languages’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Polyglot.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A polyglot is a person who knows and is able to use several languages. (बहुभाषाविद्)
◦ Example: As a polyglot, she conducted the negotiations without an interpreter.

 

• The word is built from Greek poly- (many) + glotta (tongue, language) — literally “many-tongued”. The same second element gives glossary and epiglottis.

 

• The definition specifies several languages, which is what separates the answer from the commonest distractor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Bilingual (द्विभाषी): able to speak two languages — too narrow for the definition given.

 

• Option 3: Philologist (भाषाविज्ञानी): a scholar who studies the history and structure of languages — which need not involve speaking them.

 

• Option 4: Calligrapher (सुलेखक): one skilled in beautiful handwriting.

 

NOTE

 

• The prefix poly- recurs in polygamy, polygon, polytheist, polymath (a person of wide learning) and polyandry — a family SSC returns to every year.

question:
Select the correct phrasal verb:

 

The two sides finally managed to ____ their remaining differences and sign the agreement.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. iron out.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ‘To iron out’ means to settle small difficulties or disagreements so that a plan can go forward. (मतभेद सुलझाना)
◦ Complete sentence: The two sides finally managed to iron out their remaining differences and sign the agreement.
◦ Example: A few clauses still have to be ironed out before the contract is ready.

 

• The image is that of smoothing creases out of cloth — the difficulties are wrinkles in an otherwise finished agreement, and the word finally in the sentence confirms that they were removed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘hand out’ means to distribute — The volunteers handed out relief packets.

 

• Option 3: ‘hold out’ means to resist, or to offer a hope — The garrison held out for a week.

 

• Option 4: ‘make out’ means to manage to see, hear or understand something with difficulty — I could barely make out his signature.

 

NOTE

 

• Phrasal verbs of settling and resolving: sort out (to organise or resolve), patch up (to repair a quarrel), thrash out (to discuss until agreement is reached), smooth over (to make a disagreement seem less serious).

question:
Select the correct option:

 

In the light of the fresh evidence, the earlier verdict came to be regarded with growing ____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. scepticism.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Scepticism (noun) means an attitude of doubt about whether something is true or reliable. (संदेह, शंका)
◦ Complete sentence: In the light of the fresh evidence, the earlier verdict came to be regarded with growing scepticism.

 

• Two clues fix the answer. ‘Fresh evidence’ implies that the old conclusion has been unsettled, and the adjective ‘growing’ suits a doubt that increases as the new facts accumulate.

 

• The collocation itself is worth noting: one regards a claim with scepticism, and views it with suspicion, with alarm or with approval.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Conviction (दृढ़ विश्वास): a firm belief — the reverse of what new contrary evidence produces.

 

• Option 3: Approval (अनुमोदन): a favourable opinion, which the context does not support.

 

• Option 4: Certainty (निश्चय): freedom from doubt — again the opposite of the sense required.

 

NOTE

 

• In such questions, read the modifier before choosing. Words like growing, mounting, lingering suit doubts and misgivings, while firm, unshakeable, quiet suit belief and confidence.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

There were less applicants this year (1)/ than there had been in the previous session, (2)/ although the number of vacancies (3)/ had actually been increased. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ‘Less’ is used with uncountable nouns, and ‘fewer’ with countable nouns in the plural. Applicants can be counted, so the correct word is fewer.
◦ Corrected: There were fewer applicants this year than there had been in the previous session, although the number of vacancies had actually been increased.

 

• A simple test: if the noun can take a number before it (ten applicants), use fewer; if it cannot (less water, less time, less information), use less.

 

• The plural verb were is correct here, since the subject that follows There is the plural applicants.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct: the past perfect had been rightly refers to the earlier session.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the number of vacancies is a well-formed singular subject.

 

• Part (4) is correct: had actually been increased is a properly formed past perfect passive.

 

NOTE

 

• The parallel pairs to memorise: much / many, less / fewer, amount of / number of, little / few. The first of each pair goes with uncountable nouns, the second with countable ones.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

The management offered the workers a substantial bonus.
option_1: The workers were offered a substantial bonus by the management.
option_2: A substantial bonus was offering to the workers by the management.
option_3: The workers have been offered a substantial bonus by the management.
option_4: The workers were offering a substantial bonus by the management.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The workers were offered a substantial bonus by the management.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb offer takes two objects — an indirect object (the workers) and a direct object (a substantial bonus). Either may become the subject of the passive, but the more natural and the more commonly tested form makes the person the subject.
◦ Passive: The workers were offered a substantial bonus by the management.

 

• The tense must be preserved: offered is simple past, so the passive auxiliary is were, agreeing with the new plural subject the workers.

 

• The alternative passive is equally correct in grammar — A substantial bonus was offered to the workers by the management — but note that it requires the preposition to before the person.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses was offering, an active continuous form, in place of the passive was offered.

 

• Option 3 shifts the tense to the present perfect, which the original does not warrant.

 

• Option 4 makes the workers do the offering, reversing the sense entirely.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs with two objects — give, offer, pay, teach, send, lend, promise, award, tell — allow two passives. Remember to insert to or for when the thing becomes the subject: A bonus was offered to the workers.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The general manager was extremely annoyed (1)/ with the delay in the delivery (2)/ and refused to accept (3)/ any further explanation from the supplier. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective annoyed takes with before a person, but at or by before a thing or a situation. Here the cause is the delay, so the correct preposition is at.
◦ Corrected: The general manager was extremely annoyed at the delay in the delivery and refused to accept any further explanation from the supplier.
◦ Example: He was annoyed with the clerk, and annoyed at the mistake.

 

• The same distinction governs a whole family of adjectives of feeling: angry with a person but angry at a thing; pleased with a person but pleased at an outcome.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: extremely annoyed is a well-formed adjective phrase.

 

• Part (3) is correct: refused to accept rightly takes the infinitive.

 

• Part (4) is correct: from the supplier is the appropriate preposition after accept.

 

NOTE

 

• Prepositions after adjectives of feeling: angry with / at, anxious about, ashamed of, jealous of, grateful to a person for a thing, surprised at, disappointed with / at, content with.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The annual fair at the temple ground drew crowds from three districts.
option_1: The village fair lasted for a fortnight after the harvest.
option_2: Stalls of every kind were set up at the fair.
option_3: The accused was assured of a fair trial by the court.
option_4: A wheel of the giant swing broke down during the fair.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The accused was assured of a fair trial by the court.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, fair is a noun meaning a gathering of stalls and amusements held periodically. (मेला)

 

• In Option 3, fair is an adjective meaning just, impartial and free from bias. (न्यायसंगत, निष्पक्ष) That is a wholly different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The other three options all use fair in the sense of a fairground gathering, exactly as the highlighted word does.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: the village fair lasted a fortnight — the same sense as the given sentence.

 

• Option 2: stalls set up at the fair — again the gathering.

 

• Option 4: during the fair — the same sense once more.

 

NOTE

 

• The word has further senses — light in colour (fair hair) and moderately good (a fair chance) — and a homophone, fare (the money paid for a journey, or food). Both are regularly set in SSC papers.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The results of the written examination will be declared by the board next month.
option_1: The board declares the results of the written examination next month.
option_2: The board will declare the results of the written examination next month.
option_3: The board is going to be declaring the results of the written examination next month.
option_4: The board would have declared the results of the written examination next month.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The board will declare the results of the written examination next month.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — the board — becomes the subject of the active sentence, and the passive subject the results becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb will be declared is in the simple future, so the active verb is will declare. The adverbial next month stays where it is.
◦ Active: The board will declare the results of the written examination next month.

 

• Rule for the simple future: will be + V3 (passive) ↔ will + V1 (active). The auxiliary be disappears in the active voice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the simple present declares, which cannot express a plain future intention here.

 

• Option 3 replaces the simple future with a clumsy future continuous of intention.

 

• Option 4 uses would have declared, which suggests an action that in fact never took place.

 

NOTE

 

• In voice-change questions, first identify the tense of the auxiliary, then rebuild the verb around it. Changing the voice must never change the tense, the number of the verb’s subject apart.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

Her elder sister was married with a doctor from Pune last winter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. married to a doctor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb marry takes the preposition to when the spouse is named: one is married to somebody, never married with.
◦ Corrected: Her elder sister was married to a doctor from Pune last winter.
◦ Example: She has been married to him for twelve years.

 

• Note also that marry used as an ordinary verb takes no preposition at all: He married her last year — not married with her.

 

• The preposition by is used only for the person who performs the ceremony: They were married by the registrar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the wrong preposition and adds a definite article for which the sentence gives no warrant.

 

• Option 3 uses a continuous form and still keeps to after marrying, which is not the required structure.

 

• Option 4 would mean that the doctor conducted the wedding.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs whose prepositions are commonly mistaken under Indian usage: married to (not with), discuss (no about), enter (no into for a place), request (no for), comprise (no of), resemble (no with).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The two brothers resemble with each other so closely that visitors often confuse them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. resemble each other.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Resemble is a transitive verb and takes its object directly, without any preposition. One resembles somebody, not resembles with or resembles to somebody.
◦ Corrected: The two brothers resemble each other so closely that visitors often confuse them.
◦ Example: The copy resembles the original in every detail.

 

• The corresponding noun does take a preposition — He bears a strong resemblance to his father — which is the source of the confusion tested here.

 

• Resemble is also a stative verb and is not normally used in the continuous form; are resembling is therefore doubly wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 replaces one wrong preposition with another.

 

• Option 3 keeps with and adds an unacceptable continuous form.

 

• Option 4 merely exchanges each other for one another while retaining the error.

 

NOTE

 

• Transitive verbs that need no preposition: resemble, discuss, enter, marry, reach, order, attack, accompany, comprise, emphasise, investigate, describe (though describe needs to before a person).

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India draws more groundwater than any other country, and the paradox of its water policy is that the more the state has invested in securing irrigation, the less secure the water table has become. Canal networks and cheap electricity for pumping were meant to free the cultivator from the uncertainty of the monsoon; across large parts of the north-west they have instead produced a dependence deeper than the one they replaced. A tubewell is private, immediate and unmetered, and every farmer who deepens his bore acts for reasons that are entirely rational at the level of his own field and ruinous at the level of the aquifer. The difficulty is not merely technical. Groundwater in Indian law has long been treated as an attribute of the land above it, so that the right to draw is limited chiefly by the depth one can afford to drill. That rule quietly converts a common resource into a private one, and it favours whoever has the capital for a deeper pump; small holders, unable to chase a falling table, end by buying water from their neighbours at rates the market alone decides. Cropping patterns compound the problem. Procurement policy has for decades guaranteed a price for water-intensive crops in precisely those districts least able to support them, so that the signals reaching the farmer point away from what his land can sustain. To blame the cultivator for responding to those signals is to mistake a symptom for a cause. Recharge alone will not settle the account either: a structure that captures rainwater is of little use where the extraction that empties the aquifer continues unmeasured. What has shown results, in Andhra Pradesh and elsewhere, is participatory measurement — farmers themselves reading the water levels in their own wells, sharing the figures openly, and agreeing collectively on what may be sown. A rule imposed from above is resented and evaded; a limit the users have set for themselves is far harder to ignore.

 

According to the passage, what is the main paradox of India’s water policy?
option_1: Rainfall has declined steadily across the north-west
option_2: Investment meant to reduce uncertainty has left the water table less secure
option_3: Farmers have refused to adopt tubewell technology
option_4: Canal networks have been abandoned in favour of rivers
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Investment meant to reduce uncertainty has left the water table less secure.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paradox is stated in the opening sentence: the more the state has invested in securing irrigation, the less secure the water table has become.

 

• The next line explains the mechanism — canals and cheap power for pumping were meant to free the farmer from the monsoon, but have produced a dependence deeper than the one they replaced. The remedy itself became the cause.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces a claim about rainfall that the passage never makes.

 

• Option 3 reverses the text — the difficulty arises precisely because tubewells are so widely adopted.

 

• Option 4 invents an abandonment of canals that is nowhere mentioned.

 

NOTE

 

• A paradox always contains a reversal of expectation. Look for the sentence built on the more … the less, yet, or instead, and the answer will normally be a restatement of it.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

That rule quietly converts a common resource into a private one, and it favours whoever has the capital for a deeper pump; small holders, unable to chase a falling table, end by buying water from their neighbours at rates the market alone decides. Cropping patterns compound the problem. Procurement policy has for decades guaranteed a price for water-intensive crops in precisely those districts least able to support them, so that the signals reaching the farmer point away from what his land can sustain. To blame the cultivator for responding to those signals is to mistake a symptom for a cause. Recharge alone will not settle the account either: a structure that captures rainwater is of little use where the extraction that empties the aquifer continues unmeasured. What has shown results, in Andhra Pradesh and elsewhere, is participatory measurement — farmers themselves reading the water levels in their own wells, sharing the figures openly, and agreeing collectively on what may be sown. A rule imposed from above is resented and evaded; a limit the users have set for themselves is far harder to ignore.

 

Why, according to the passage, do small holders end up buying water from their neighbours?
option_1: Because no aquifer lies beneath their fields
option_2: Because the law forbids them to sink a bore of their own
option_3: Because they cannot afford to keep drilling deeper as the table falls
option_4: Because their neighbours sell water below the market rate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Because they cannot afford to keep drilling deeper as the table falls.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage explains that the right to draw groundwater is limited chiefly by the depth one can afford to drill, which favours whoever has the capital for a deeper pump.

 

• The consequence follows in the same sentence: small holders, unable to chase a falling table, end by buying water from neighbours at rates the market alone decides — that is, at whatever price the seller can command.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is nowhere suggested; the water exists but lies beyond their reach.

 

• Option 2 reverses the law as described — the right to draw is barely restricted at all.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage, in which the price is set by the market and works against the buyer.

 

NOTE

 

• Cause-and-effect questions are usually answered by a single sentence containing both. Locate the phrase that names the group in the question — here small holders — and read the clause attached to it.

Which of the following does NOT, as per the passage, contribute to the depletion of groundwater?
option_3: Treating groundwater as an attribute of the land above it
option_4: Farmers reading and sharing the water levels of their own wells
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Farmers reading and sharing the water levels of their own wells.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is a negative question, so the answer is the option the passage presents as a remedy rather than a cause. Participatory measurement — farmers reading their own wells, sharing the figures and agreeing on what may be sown — is named as what has shown results.

 

• The other three are all listed among the causes:
◦ the tubewell is private, immediate and unmetered;
◦ procurement policy guarantees a price for water-intensive crops in the districts least able to support them;
◦ treating groundwater as an attribute of the land converts a common resource into a private one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 appears in the first paragraph, in the description of the tubewell.

 

• Option 2 appears in the paragraph on cropping patterns.

 

• Option 3 appears in the discussion of the legal rule.

 

NOTE

 

• With ‘which does NOT’ questions, tick off in the margin every option you can trace to the passage. The one that remains untraceable — or that belongs to the solution rather than the problem — is the answer.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India draws more groundwater than any other country, and the paradox of its water policy is that the more the state has invested in securing irrigation, the less secure the water table has become. Canal networks and cheap electricity for pumping were meant to free the cultivator from the uncertainty of the monsoon; across large parts of the north-west they have instead produced a dependence deeper than the one they replaced. A tubewell is private, immediate and unmetered, and every farmer who deepens his bore acts for reasons that are entirely rational at the level of his own field and ruinous at the level of the aquifer. The difficulty is not merely technical. Groundwater in Indian law has long been treated as an attribute of the land above it, so that the right to draw is limited chiefly by the depth one can afford to drill. That rule quietly converts a common resource into a private one, and it favours whoever has the capital for a deeper pump; small holders, unable to chase a falling table, end by buying water from their neighbours at rates the market alone decides. Cropping patterns compound the problem. Procurement policy has for decades guaranteed a price for water-intensive crops in precisely those districts least able to support them, so that the signals reaching the farmer point away from what his land can sustain. To blame the cultivator for responding to those signals is to mistake a symptom for a cause. Recharge alone will not settle the account either: a structure that captures rainwater is of little use where the extraction that empties the aquifer continues unmeasured. What has shown results, in Andhra Pradesh and elsewhere, is participatory measurement — farmers themselves reading the water levels in their own wells, sharing the figures openly, and agreeing collectively on what may be sown. A rule imposed from above is resented and evaded; a limit the users have set for themselves is far harder to ignore.

 

What assumption does the author criticise?
option_1: That building recharge structures alone can restore the aquifer
option_2: That farmers are indifferent to the scarcity of water
option_3: That canal irrigation is cheaper than tubewell irrigation
option_4: That state governments are unwilling to frame any rules
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. That building recharge structures alone can restore the aquifer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that recharge alone will not settle the account: a structure that captures rainwater is of little use where the extraction that empties the aquifer continues unmeasured.

 

• The criticism is therefore of a half-measure — adding water at one end while leaving withdrawal at the other end uncounted. It is the assumption of sufficiency, not the practice of recharge itself, that the author rejects.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is contradicted by the passage, which insists that the farmer acts rationally and should not be blamed.

 

• Option 3 raises a comparison of costs that the passage never makes.

 

• Option 4 misreads the closing lines, which concern how rules work, not whether they are framed.

 

NOTE

 

• Words such as ‘alone’, ‘merely’ and ‘by itself’ are the author’s signal that a popular remedy is about to be called insufficient. The sentence containing them usually holds the criticised assumption.

A rule imposed from above is resented and evaded; a limit the users have set for themselves is far harder to ignore.

 

What is implied about rules imposed from above?
option_1: They are the only workable remedy for over-extraction
option_2: They succeed less well than limits the users set for themselves
option_3: They have never been attempted anywhere in India
option_4: They are chiefly opposed by large landholders
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. They succeed less well than limits the users set for themselves.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The final sentence draws the contrast explicitly: a rule imposed from above is resented and evaded, whereas a limit the users have set for themselves is far harder to ignore.

 

• The point is one of compliance, not of legality. The passage does not say that regulation is wrong, only that ownership of the limit decides whether it is obeyed — which is why participatory measurement is offered as the example that has worked.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 states the reverse of the author’s conclusion.

 

• Option 3 is an absolute claim the passage never makes.

 

• Option 4 names a group whose opposition the passage does not discuss.

 

NOTE

 

• The last sentence of an argumentative passage very often carries the implication being tested. Read it against each option before deciding.

question:
Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below.

 

The engineer explained that, were the load increased beyond that point, the beam would fail without warning.
option_1: The engineer said, “If the load is increased beyond this point, the beam will fail without warning.”
option_2: The engineer said, “Were the load increased beyond this point, the beam would fail without warning.”
option_3: The engineer said, “Had the load been increased beyond this point, the beam would have failed without warning.”
option_4: The engineer said, “The beam will fail without warning if the load would be increased beyond this point.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The engineer said, “Were the load increased beyond this point, the beam would fail without warning.”

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported clause is a second conditional in its inverted form (were the load increased … would fail). Conditionals of this kind are already unreal, and therefore do not change when speech is reported — which means nothing has to be undone when converting back.

 

• Only two changes are required: the connective that is dropped in favour of inverted commas, and the demonstrative that point returns to this point, since the speaker is now speaking in the immediate situation.
◦ Direct: The engineer said, “Were the load increased beyond this point, the beam would fail without warning.”

 

• The inversion itself belongs to the structure of the sentence and is carried across unchanged.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 converts the sentence into a first conditional, turning an unreal supposition into a likely event.

 

• Option 3 turns it into a third conditional, which would describe an unreal past.

 

• Option 4 places would inside the if-clause, which no conditional permits.

 

NOTE

 

• Unchanged in reported speech: second and third conditionals, universal truths, habitual facts, and the modals would, could, might, should, ought to. Only the pronouns and the adverbs of time and place are adjusted.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said, “I met her at the conference last year.”
option_1: He said that he met her at the conference last year.
option_2: He said that he had met her at the conference the previous year.
option_3: He said that he has met her at the conference the previous year.
option_4: He said that he had been meeting her at the conference last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He said that he had met her at the conference the previous year.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb said is in the past, so the reported verb is back-shifted one step: the simple past met becomes the past perfect had met.

 

• The time expression must also change: last year becomes the previous year (or the year before), since the moment of speaking is no longer the present.
◦ Indirect: He said that he had met her at the conference the previous year.

 

• The connective that replaces the inverted commas, and the pronoun I becomes he.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves both the tense and the time expression untouched.

 

• Option 3 uses the present perfect after a past reporting verb, which the sequence of tenses forbids.

 

• Option 4 turns a single completed meeting into a repeated or continuing one.

 

NOTE

 

• Time expressions in reported speech: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, last year → the previous year, next month → the following month, ago → before.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The old iron bridge over the river was declared unsafe one summer and closed to all traffic.

 

A. Schoolchildren from the far bank now walked eleven kilometres each way to reach a working crossing.

 

B. The engineers’ report had recommended immediate replacement, but no allocation followed for four years.

 

C. Within a month a light footbridge of steel rope hung across the narrowest point of the channel.

 

D. It was the parents, and not the department, who at last collected the money and hired a contractor.

 

S2. The official bridge, when it came two years later, was built beside a crossing the village had already made for itself.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-A-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – D – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from closure → official inaction → hardship → local initiative → result.

 

• S1 reports the closure.
◦ B describes what the authorities did about it — a report, and then four years of nothing.
◦ A shows the consequence for the villagers; the adverb now marks the state of affairs created by the closure and the delay.
◦ D introduces the local initiative, and its emphatic phrasing (It was the parents, and not the department) is meaningful only after the department’s inaction in B has been described.
◦ C gives the result of that initiative, within a month, and leads into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-D-C) places the villagers’ long detour before the delay that caused it.

 

• Option 3 (B-D-A-C) has the parents act before the hardship has been shown.

 

• Option 4 (A-D-B-C) leaves the contrast in D without the official inaction it depends on.

 

NOTE

 

• An emphatic contrast such as It was X, and not Y, who … must follow the sentence that establishes what Y failed to do. Locate the contrast first, and the sentence before it is fixed.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The postage stamp began as the answer to a problem of accounting rather than of transport.

 

A. Clerks spent more time calculating charges by distance and by the number of sheets than in moving the mail at all.

 

B. Postage was then paid by the recipient, who remained free to refuse a letter and pay nothing whatever.

 

C. Refused letters had therefore been carried twice at the office’s expense, and the losses were considerable.

 

D. A single prepaid adhesive label removed both difficulties at once, and the rate was made uniform for the whole country.

 

S2. Within a few years the same small device had been copied by post offices across the world.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A-B-C-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – B – C – D – S2, and the paragraph moves from first difficulty → second difficulty → its consequence → the single remedy.

 

• S1 announces a problem of accounting.
◦ A gives the first difficulty — the labour of calculating charges — which is exactly an accounting problem and so follows S1 directly.
◦ B introduces the second difficulty: payment fell on the recipient, who could refuse.
◦ C begins with “Refused letters … therefore”, and both the noun and the connective tie it firmly to B.
◦ D supplies the remedy and speaks of “both difficulties”, a phrase that requires two difficulties to have been named already — so D must come last.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (B-A-C-D) separates C from B, although Refused letters depends on the refusal described in B.

 

• Option 3 (A-C-B-D) mentions refused letters before the right of refusal has been introduced.

 

• Option 4 (B-C-A-D) postpones the accounting difficulty that S1 has already announced.

 

NOTE

 

• A phrase such as “both difficulties”, “all three reasons” or “either course” counts for you: the sentence containing it must come after every item it counts, and is therefore almost always last.
